product_title: Razer Viper V4 Pro Wireless Esports Gaming Mouse, 49g,180Hr Battery, Black
headline: Great Gaming Mouse for 2026
review_text_raw: This is the best gaming mouse as someone who upgraded from a regular stock mouse. The weight, the functionality, and the design of the mouse is perfect. In fact, this mouse, and it features had further fine-tuned my already decent aim. After using this mouse for a while, I have observed my aim became a natural aim bot, where I was even accused of potentially exploiting in a match of BF1. The mouse itself is light, and as someone who came from a heavier mouse it felt a bit weird at first. However, if you can manage it, then it becomes a benefit. It allows you to flick quickly, and track targets consistently, which is where my claim of "natural aim bot" came from. It's not too light where you might find yourself tensing up too much to keep it in place, but if you came from a heavier mouse, then you might overflick your target a few times. The features the mouse offered through Razer's Synapse software such as the DPI and mappings are very useful. You can set different profiles for different games, so there are different DPI's for each game. In addition, you can change the mouse's buttons to be mapped to keys on your keyboard. For example, you can have the side button mapped to 'R', so you can reload through the side button. You can also have the same side buttons run a macro, so if you're playing Helldivers 2, you can instantly input a stratagem through your side button. There are also features like letting the side buttons launch a program. The mouse also features polling rates up to 8k, where higher rates increases the consistency of your cursor's tracking across the screen, and decreases latency. HOWEVER, higher rates can drain the battery life faster, and require specific hardware. Increased polling rates will put higher loads onto your CPU, so ensure you have a strong enough CPU. Otherwise, CPU intensive games will suffer FPS drops, or in general, some games might have issues or do not even support said polling rates. In addition, to notice the different in polling rates, a monitor with a higher refresh rate will be required. Regardless, using 2k and 4k, I haven't really noticed a difference as someone who has a 180hz monitor. It feels the same as 1k polling rate, but if you have the hardware to support it, use it! Regarding the battery life, it's very very good. I have used 2k and 4k polling rates for hours in a day, and the battery only goes down from 100% to like 96%. Whereas if you use 1k polling rate, then the battery doesn't even drain at all till the next day or two maybe (I charge it overnight once the day ends). Upgrading from a wired mouse, and as someone who was a firm believer that wired mice was better, this mouse changed that. I found the wireless mode of this mouse more consistent, than my wired mouse, and offered more freedom in wrist/arm movement. Therefore, I was able to track better. Also, the latency was small on it, perhaps even better. However, you can use the USB cable and plug it into the mouse if you'd like to use it wired. The design of the mouse is comfortable for those who use a claw grip. I typically have my palm touching the mouse, and my fingers in a claw like stance on it. I found no discomfort, and was able to consistently aim. As for other grips, I do not know. If you're upgrading from a stock mouse, then this is worth the upgrade. However, please read other reviews, if you're upgrading from like Razer's Viper V3 Pro mouse, then it might not be worth the money. Since the V3 shares many similarities to the V4 with a few new features. Overall, this might be one of the best mice on the market right now. This mouse ended up being the final piece in the puzzle for me towards perfect aim. Somehow, my peripherals were holding me back, where it is typically the opposite.

headline: Left me Surprised in a Good Way
review_text_raw: This mouse took me by surprise. Coming from the Basilisk V3 Pro, this one is just so lightweight that I almost mistook it for a toy. I seriously can't believe how light this is. The battery life is phenomenal, and the controls are astoundingly tight. The buttons on my Basilisk always felt cheap and mushy, but every button on this Viper V4 Pro is snappy and solid. Getting to the part people care about most, this is probably the most fluid mouse I've ever used. The 50K sensor is a marketing ploy, as I don't use anything over 6400DPI, but you can turn on the 8K polling with a high refresh rate monitor and you won't see any dragging of your cursor across your screen as you will with lower refresh rates, and the higher polling rate shows your mouse's location on the screen more times per second than traditional 1K polling rates. My eyes can see the difference, but only if I strain to see it. I run the mouse at 1K polling rate for optimal battery life and because most games are using that rate the most effectively. It's a sweet spot. So the reasons to get the mouse are simple: lightweight, long battery life, no skipping, truly ambidextrous. The cons: no wireless charging, and no RGB. But those are apparent tradeoffs for that impossibly light 49 gram feel.

product_title: Razer Viper V4 Pro Wireless Esports Gaming Mouse, 49g,180Hr Battery, Black
headline: Is it worth the upgrade?
review_text_raw: The Razer Viper V4 Pro is a flagship-level esports mouse that doubles down on performance rather than reinventing the formula. It features an ultra-lightweight ambidextrous design at around 49–50g, paired with Razer’s Focus Pro 50K optical sensor capable of 50,000 DPI, 930 IPS tracking, and 90G acceleration. It also introduces Gen-4 optical switches, improved wireless performance with an upgraded dongle, and up to 180 hours of battery life. On paper, it’s one of the most technically refined mice available fast, consistent, and clearly built for competitive play. That said, if you already own the Razer Viper V3 Pro, there’s honestly no real reason to upgrade. The improvements here are incremental slightly better battery life, marginally upgraded switches, and small refinements that you’re not going to feel in-game. The V3 Pro is already insanely lightweight, responsive, and accurate, so the V4 Pro ends up feeling more like a spec bump than a meaningful evolution. Unless you’re chasing absolute top-end specs for the sake of it, you’re better off sticking with the V3 Pro. As a stand alone mouse, I give it 4 stars. As a "upgrade" to the previous generation I'd give it one star.

product_title: Razer Viper V4 Pro Wireless Esports Gaming Mouse, 49g,180Hr Battery, Black
headline: New main. Excellent mouse with a ridiculous battery life
review_text_raw: The box didn't have much protection, but it arrived in great condition. As for the mouse itself, it is amazing. I won't talk much about shape because that's highly subjective (I'll just say it fits my hand size and grip style), but everything else is excellent: coating is smooth and grippy, very nice to the touch; main clicks are light and tactile, tho they could have a little less post travel; side buttons are well tensioned and positioned; the wheel might be the weakest aspect, because the scrolling feels a bit off, but it's totally functional; M3 click is very tactile; skates are smooth and fast; build quality is perfect, solid as a rock; performance is top tier, no complaints; and finally, the battery is absolutely insane. I have been using the mouse for 12 days at 1000hz (sometimes 8000, but only for a couple of Apex matches) and it has only gone down to 60%. On top of all of that, Razer has finally made a web software. That means 2 things: 1) you don't have to deal with the bloatware that is Synapse (except for firmware updates); and 2) you can change your settings on Linux, which has been a game changer for me (I dual boot Windows 11 and Bazzite). I think it is worth the price, but only if you don't have a Viper V3 Pro (or even a Viper V3 Pro SE). On paper, the V4 Pro has many improvements, but the only real upgrade that a player will notice is the battery life and the web software. I recommend it to people who have never owned a Viper V3 and want the latest technology and power efficiency. I can recommend it to those who just want to try the shape, but they might also want to take a look at the V3 Pro, since it is cheaper right now.

product_title: Razer Naga V2 HyperSpeed Wireless MMO Gaming Mouse, 400 Hr Battery, Black
headline: Best mouse I've owned.
review_text_raw: After my Logitech G604 at work decided to start having switch troubles, it was time to look for another mouse. I was hoping to get another Logitech G604 or similar since I utilize the side buttons for work and for gaming. Unfortunately, at least as of the last time I searched, Logitech discontinued the G604 and didn't plan on making another similar. I'm glad I started looking at Razer mice as this one caught my eye and I was intrigued. I've had this mouse now for 9 months and it was the best decision I've made in any of my PC purchases, minus the PC of course. The mouse feels good in your hand and is very light compared to the G604. The feet slide extremely easy on mouse pads for flawless movement. The buttons are very responsive and I enjoy the extra 6 that I get compared to the 604; more commands/shortcuts at a thumb press. Some have had the button paint start to wear off but I have not, at least yet, so I'm not sure if they just have super acidic hand sweat or eating Cheetos while gaming. Anywho, the paint has not worn off in any way and I can still read all the numbers on the side buttons. As far as connectivity, I don't 'hardcore' game so I probably won't ever use the HyperSpeed setting on it but the bluetooth works wonderfully and is very quick to connect on start up. The mouse also has a timeout function which you can adjust via the software. The software I don't hear much good about but I haven't had trouble with it I guess. It allows me to program the buttons as needed and that's about all I use it for since this is the only Razer product I have. I'd recommend this mouse to anyone who doesn't like searching for keys on their keyboard for functions. It's not only a great mouse for gaming but for work when you need button combos that are a pain to do on the keyboard. I liked it so much that I ended up buying another one for home and replaced my G604 at home a few months later.

headline: Razer is back on top! Naga V2 is awesome.
review_text_raw: I used to despise Razer, but nowadays, the MMO mouse from Razer is pretty decent hardware. Their biggest problem has always been their software, however, and I must admit their support for software integrations is lacking. There's no OBS integration and no Discord integration. I'm getting by without setting up macros for hotkey combos by simply using my Logitech keyboard's macro keys for the integrations I want, and the only reason I didn't get another Logitech mouse was Logitech didn't make a new mouse model and discontinued their old, wired G600 model, making it cost too much to replace. I went with the Razer Naga V2 because it was somewhat cheap by comparison and wireless and I felt like giving other brands a try. I ended up really loving the build quality of the Naga V2, but Razer's software was still pretty terrible. The hardware design is pretty good, but there are some ergonomics issues. The top left mouse click buttons (not left click) are hard to find by feel and also a little difficult to reach. There's no palm rest for a big hand to rest on. I think this mouse could benefit greatly from a 3d printable palm extension, but that would increase its weight, and the mouse is very lightweight. I ended up using a wrist rest that helped a little with mouse fatigue. The battery is somewhat easy to swap out, and you don't have to swap often. It uses a single AA battery, and I opted to use a rechargeable lithium battery in it that adds some extra capacity. The LEDs on the buttons are very dim by comparison to my other MMO mice, and they don't have the same flair I get from some other brands. The colors are customizable, but there's no wave effect on the mouse, which is weird because Razer's keyboards have the wave effect. DPI is easy to change on-the-fly. I see no noticeable lag from being wireless. I also don't see any connectivity issues as long as I keep the mouse within 8 feet of its dongle.

headline: I don't know how I ever lived without it.
review_text_raw: I'm very happy with this device. My laptop doesn't have an ethernet port and only has one USB-C SuperSpeed port, so I bought an ethernet to USB-C cable to connect my ethernet switch to the Anker and into my laptop's USB-C port, and it works great. I don't need a fast internet connection for the things I do, so my service is only a 50mbps symmetrical up/down connection, and that's what I get even while transferring files from my external between other devices, charging my phone, and using composite devices. I bought the Anker 100W Compact and Foldable USB C Charger for it and it charges my S24 extremely fast. It's very well built, yet super lightweight. I love the sleek, slender design. It's the perfect size to easily slide into a pocket, store in a desk drawer, or keep handy in a laptop case or backpack. Using it is easy. Just plug it into your computer and plug your devices into it. Just make sure you have a power supply for it if you're charging or powering other devices, using external storage, or running anything else that taxes USB power. I have had ZERO connectivity issues with it — no random disconnect/reconnect blips, no failed transfers for huge amounts of data that have taken up to 45 minutes, no static his or crackle when my headset is running through it... no problems at all. It's actually kind of spooky now that I think about it... I can't recall a time I've ever had a similar device that didn't have some nuance that got under my skin, like a loose connection, random disconnections, having to reinstall the drivers all the time, or having to troubleshoot just to get it connected for the first time. The most stress I've put it through was with my keyboard connected, ethernet running through it, my S24 charging and transferring about ~20gb of pictures and videos to my 2T external HD at the same time that my laptop was transferring about ~500gb of media and documents to the HD, too, and I was surprised by how warm it DIDN'T get. My only complaint is trivial and unique to my situation — I wish output cord was longer. About six inches would do. My laptop sits up on an adjustable stand that clamps to my desk, and the end where the output cord is hangs a few inches off of my desk. This puts extra stress on the USB-C port and can wear it out faster or damage it. I haven't had a use for the HDMI port yet, but I eventually will. I use all of the other ports for my work and personal devices, though. These include: a 2tb external hard drive; a Poly Blackwire 3320 Series headset; a dongle for a wireless mouse/keyboard combo or a wired keyboard and a dongle for a wireless mouse; my Galaxy S24 charges and transfers files through it super fast; I have several thumb drives ranging from 20gb to 512gb that I regularly use; I recently bought an RCA/S Video-to-USB converter to digitize old home movies I plug into it, too.

product_title: Belkin 100W 10Gbps Multiport USB-C Hub Adapter for Laptop, iPad, PC, & More
headline: A hub is not a dock. This is a very good USB-C hub
review_text_raw: Does what a hub ought to do - which is to say, you can plug it into one USB-C port and it will make power and data connectivity available to four downstream USB-C devices. The big caveats are that the host cable is extremely short and the power made available to downstream devices is significantly reduced from what the host provides. It's still a five star device because these short cables are universally present on all USB-C hubs, and the power limitations are less severe than other similar products that I have tested. Most importantly, the data connectivity offered by this unit is excellent, and it's extremely portable, being barely larger than the connectors it contains. I would still very much prefer a version of this device with a USB-C female connector on the back instead of the permanently attached short cable but apparently there are valid technical reasons that USB-C hubs are not made in this way. Devices that offer more power and better cabling options are now classified as docks rather than hubs, they tend to be based on Thunderbolt rather than plain old USB-C, and some of these docks are quite excellent, but they are comparatively very expensive. This particular device is just a hub, it is very affordable compared to a dock, and it's as good as USB-C hubs get.

I have a LITE-ON USB 2.0 External CD/DVD Writer Model eUAU108, manufactured in 2013, with an attached cable that is slightly less than 4 inches long. This model was an improvement over prior models, in that it requires only a single USB 2.0 connection, whereas previous models employed a Y-cable to enable connecting to 2 USB ports simultaneously for additional power. I have always felt that this drive was marginally capable of running on the 500 mA specification for USB 2.0 ports. I think this is the main reason for the ultra short cable - to minimize the voltage drop. The short cable worked OK when I was using the drive with a laptop, but attempting to use it with a computer attached to the back of my flat screen monitor is a major problem. The USB ports are about a foot above the desktop, making it necessary to support the drive in some manner. This has always been problematic. I tried using the only USB extension cable that I had, a cheap dollar store cable, and it did not work at all. My next thought was that I should purchase a higher quality, and obviously more expensive, USB cable, but I still had reservations. Would a longer cable, even of a higher quality, work? Why did LITE-ON force a short cable onto the consumer? They could have provided a USB port instead of an attached cable. I then thought of using a powered hub, which could solve the voltage/power issue, but I still wondered if there might be other signal quality issues that a longer cable might cause. I believe I was starting to overthink the matter at this point! I started looking at the market of powered hubs and discovered that there was quite a variety, from no-name cheapies to surprisingly expensive higher end units. It was easy to eliminate the no-name cheapies because there were brand names I was familiar with that were very affordable. Then I discovered that some of the hubs were rated at 10 Gbps! Gotta have that feature, right? Even though I don't have a single device faster than 5 Gbps, I justified this feature on the basis of future-proofing. I figured it would only be a matter of time before I had devices of that speed. Later on I discovered that all the USB ports on the computer attached to the back of my monitor are 10 Gbps capable – five are USB 3.2 Gen2 (10 Gbps) and one is USB4 (40 Gbps!) - additional justification for going with a 10 Gbps hub. As I looked at the 10 Gbps offerings I quickly discovered that many, if not most of them, were from RSHTECH/Rosonway. They have quite a variety of well designed, useful devices. So many options that I found it helpful to generate a table of features to more easily compare them. I finally decided to go with the RSH-H7C4 for the following reasons: • 10 Gbps on every port • both USB-A and USB-C ports • push button switch (vs. rocker type), with an indicator light, for each port • all ports support USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2), delivering a maximum of 1.5A at 5V (7.5W) per port [standard USB ports limit current to 0.5A (USB 2.0) or 0.9A (USB 3.2)] • 36W (12V/3A) DC power adapter • detachable 3.3 foot USB-C host cable (when I need to connect to a USB-A host I use a cheap adapter I purchased at a dollar store; some of the Rosonway units include a dual-headed cable with both A and C plugs!) • two year warranty It's a beautifully designed unit with a solid, weighty feel to it. Rounded edges and a thin accent band of non-anodized aluminum around each end give this hub a modern, classy appearance. With the case being narrow and slightly rounded on the bottom, one might have concern about its stability against the pushing and pulling of the connected USB cables. While it might technically be more stable with a completely flat bottom, it is surprisingly stable as is due to its weight and mass. Not at all like some of the lighter weight plastic cased devices that I have. It would take a deliberate effort to tip it over; I don't think that will be an issue. I actually do tip it over to accommodate one of my situations: the cable on my DVD drive is so short that the drive cannot lay flat when the cable is inserted into the port on the hub from above. I have to lay the hub on its side (see video). The included USB cable is heavy gauge, very thick. With my limited experience in the world of USB cables I have made two observations: 1)there is a tremendous range of cost, quality, and capabilities among the many cables on the market; 2)an extra USB cable frequently comes in handy. It would make sense to me that RSHTECH would provide a suitably high-grade cable with their hub in order to support the 10 Gbps data rate and the BC1.2 current draw capability. The fact that the USB cable is detachable is a bonus! It can be used elsewhere. I could even change it into an extension cable by the use of a gender-changing adapter. The indicator lights are a beautiful blue, quite small, but tastefull in my opinion; apparently too small for some reviewers, but I have no complaint. I would rather have them understated than overstated. The first testing I did was to connect the aforementioned LITE-ON CD/DVD writer to the computer hanging on the back of my monitor using the RSH-H7C4 hub and its included USB cable. (When the LITE-ON drive is directly attached to this computer I never have problems because the power requirement of the LITE-ON drive is easily satisfied.) I briefly tried the hub in “bus-powered” mode (without the power supply attached). I was able to read files on the DVD writer with no problem. (This was just a brief, not comprehensive, test because my main concern was testing the more power intensive task of burning a disk.) The next testing was in “self-powered” mode (with the power supply attached). I successfully burned and verified an ISO image. I then disconnected the power supply and tried to burn the image again in bus-powered mode. The burning went without any error messages, but the verification process failed. Another attempt in bus-powered mode failed during the burning process. Returning to self-powered mode (with the power supply attached), I was again able to successfully burn and verify the ISO image. It appears that when the DVD writer is attached through the hub and cable, burning a disk requires additional power beyond what the computer port is supplying (in order to power the circuitry in the hub and to compensate for loss over the length of the three foot cable). USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2) seems to do the job here. I am pleased with that! I have solved the short cable issue; I can now lay my DVD drive flat on the desk and have dependable operation. Additional testing with a much older computer, a Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 (vintage 2010), revealed an unexpected limitation: the DVD writer was unable to be recognized as a boot device by the Inspiron Mini when connected to it through the hub. As far as I can tell, this is a limitation of the older BIOS in the Inspiron. There is no way to make this system recognize an optical drive connected via a USB hub at boot up. After the system is booted the drive is able to be used with no problem. It is my understanding that the more modern BIOSes of today handle this situation in a more sophisticated manner and can detect hub-connected optical drives at bootup. I verified this by bootup tests on the computer attached to my monitor and on a modern netbook. Both of those systems were able to recognize the DVD writer at bootup with no problem when it was connected via the hub. The Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 has USB 2.0 ports that theoretically should supply enough power for the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer, but I have always felt that it was marginal. I would like to be able to supplement the power. The RSH-H7C4 is only a partial solution here. It can be used with the Inspiron for burning disks since that is a process that occurs after bootup, but in the case where I need to boot from this DVD writer I might have to first transfer the DVD image to a bootable USB thumb drive and use that instead. While not a comprehensive evaluation of the RSH-H7C4, my tests have assured me that some of my problems have been solved. I can comfortably lay the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer on the desk instead of trying to figure out how to suspend it a foot up in the air in order to attach it to the computer hanging behind my flat screen monitor. I can also use the hub for more dependable disk burning using my Inspiron Mini 1012. I am quite impressed with the RSH-H7C4 hub and RSHTECH/Rosonway. I've always been very excited by little “boxes” and devices that solve computer interconnection (and other) problems. The companies that come up with these solutions are frequently very clever. RSHTECH will now be one of the first companies I look to for such solutions. A brief look at their lineup shows devices such as: • USB switches (to share USB ports between two computers) • powered and unpowered USB hubs, some with card readers and HDMI ports • powered USB extension cables • unpowered USB extension cables with built-in signal booster chips • USB HDD/SSD enclosures • docking and cloning stations • 10 Gbps USB connected M.2 NVME/SATA SSD enclosures • 10 Gbps USB connected Magnetic M.2 NVME SSD enclosure with 100W PD RSHTECH puts an effort into including enough hard facts and specifications in their product descriptions to enable consumers to easily understand a device’s capabilities and limitations. This fact, and my favorable impression of the RSH-H7C4 hub, give me confidence to expect good performance and value with any of their products.

review_text_raw: The media could not be loaded. This device is the perfect accessory for someone needing to connect multiple devices using a single interface. Excellent for traveling light, I'm looking forward to my next trip with the need for only this charging / data hub and my laptop. Not only does this hub provide connectivity for both USB A and USB C connections, allowing me to pass data seamlessly between all of my devices without a need to repeated disconnect / reconnect for access to ports, it also CHARGES all of them simultaneously using the included 36W power supply. It was incredibly easy to decide which devices to activate with individual power switches for each port and indicators to show which ones are active. I did NOT need to deactivate any of the ports, however, as there was ample power to charge all of my equipment at one time. That means a lot when I'm traveling with early morning departures and late arrivals each day, giving me a single place to charge everything at once while I sleep and wake up ready for the next adventure. The only thing that could have made this better would have been enough power to charge my (giant) laptop, or the ability to connect a different external (USB C) power supply to make more power available. It was still a huge improvement, though, having to carry just my laptop power brick plus the adapter for this USB hub and having all the connectivity and power I need for an extended trip away from home. My backpack (and my back) really appreciate this excellently designed device. headline: Solid powered USB hub that has performed in the time I have used it.
review_text_raw: I have been in IT long enough to know that a USB hub is one of those products that sounds simple on paper but has a surprisingly wide range of quality in practice. I have also been burned enough times by bad ones to approach any new hub with a healthy dose of skepticism. So when I say that the Rosonway powered USB hub has genuinely impressed me, I want you to understand that it is coming from someone who does not hand out compliments to peripheral hardware easily. I have had this hub for 13 days now. That might not sound like a long time, but in the context of my daily IT work, I have put it through what I would consider a serious run of testing. This is not a hub that has been sitting on a desk powering a wireless mouse dongle and a phone charger. It has been put through a ringer of a minimum of 12-14 hours 5-6 days a week. And it was used every day. With a rotating cast of demanding devices that would expose any weakness in a lesser product. Why I Came Back to Rosonway This is actually my second Rosonway hub. My first one is still running, still reliable, and was purchased specifically because I had grown so frustrated with other brands that I needed something I could actually count on. Before finding Rosonway the first time, I dealt with pretty much every problem a USB hub can throw at you — and often all at once. Devices dropping connection randomly. Transfer speeds that had no business being as slow as they were, even on a nominally high-speed hub. Units that died within weeks of purchase. Build quality that felt like it might give out at any moment. When you work in IT, unreliable hardware is not just an annoyance — it is a productivity problem and, at times, a professional one. The last thing I need in the middle of a task is a hub that decides to drop a device or throttle my speeds without warning. After going through several different brands and experiencing those issues repeatedly, I finally landed on Rosonway. My first unit solved all of those problems and has kept solving them ever since. So when I needed more ports, the decision to go back to Rosonway was not really a decision at all. It was the obvious move based on earned trust. Sure you could go with more notorious brands, but the bang for my buck on this brand has been optimal. Daily Use in an IT Context My use case is not casual. I run this hub daily as part of an IT work setup that includes both a PC and a Mac, and I switch between the two regularly. Cross-platform reliability is something I specifically look for and specifically test, because a hub that works beautifully on Windows but causes headaches on macOS is only solving half my problem. This one works correctly on both. No configuration differences, no quirks on one platform that do not exist on the other. It simply works the same way on both machines, which is exactly what you want. The range of peripherals I have connected through this hub over the past 13 days is wide. I have been running a wired USB-C to 3.5mm DAC for my Corsair headset with microphone — and I want to flag this one specifically, because audio devices are often where cheaper hubs start to show their weaknesses. A DAC demands consistent, clean power delivery. Any instability shows up immediately as audio dropout, static, or microphone signal issues. This hub has delivered clean, uninterrupted audio and microphone performance every single time. Beyond that, I have put external hard drives, thumb drives, and an SSD dock through this hub. External drives and SSD docks are about the most demanding things you can connect to a USB hub from a power and bandwidth standpoint. Drives pulling sustained power while transferring data will expose any inadequacy in a hub's power management quickly. I have had no issues — transfers run at expected speeds, the SSD dock behaves as if it is connected directly to the machine, and nothing has dropped or stuttered. I have connected all of these devices in various combinations, not just one at a time. Running multiple demanding peripherals simultaneously is where a lot of hubs start to fall apart, and this one has handled every configuration I have thrown at it without complaint. No Drivers, No Nonsense One of the things I appreciated immediately was the plug-and-play experience. There were no extra drivers to hunt down and install. On both the PC and the Mac, I connected the hub and everything worked. That is the experience it should always be, but it is not always the experience you get — especially when you are working across two different operating systems. Anyone who has spent time troubleshooting driver issues for what should be a simple USB hub knows how much time that can waste. The fact that this product required none of that was noticed and appreciated from day one. The Physical Setup The cable length on this hub is one of the practical details that does not always get mentioned in reviews but genuinely matters in a real workspace. It is long enough to allow for flexible positioning without being so long that it becomes a cable management problem. I was able to position the hub where it actually needed to be on my desk rather than compromising based on where the cable could reach. Small thing, but it adds up. The hub is powered, which is worth emphasizing for anyone who has tried to run demanding devices off a bus-powered hub and wondered why things were not working right. Having dedicated power through the included adapter means each port has what it needs to perform, even with multiple devices pulling from it simultaneously. For the kind of peripherals I am running — drives, an SSD dock, a DAC — powered is not optional. It is required. This hub delivers that without any hesitation. Thirteen Days and Counting I want to be honest about what 13 days of heavy daily use tells you and what it does not. It does not give you years of long-term reliability data. What it does give you is a solid read on whether a product is going to perform under real working conditions without hand-holding. I have not been gentle with this hub, in terms of use. I have been plugging and unplugging devices frequently, running demanding transfers, switching between operating systems, and connecting combinations of peripherals that test the power distribution. In all of that, I have not encountered a single failure, dropout, connection issue, or performance problem. That tracks with my experience with my first Rosonway hub, which is still running well after a year and half. The consistency between the two units tells me something about how Rosonway approaches quality control. It is one thing for one product to perform well. It is another for two separate purchases, at different times, to both deliver the same reliable experience. Who This Hub Is For If you are running a setup with demanding peripherals — external drives, audio devices, docking solutions — and you need something that will perform reliably across PC and Mac without driver headaches or connection instability, this hub is worth serious consideration. If you have been through the frustrating cycle of buying cheaper hubs, dealing with the problems they inevitably bring, and then replacing them, I understand that cycle because I lived it for longer than I should have. The Rosonway powered USB hub is not the flashiest product in the world. It does not need to be. It has been dependable so far. It does exactly what it is supposed to do, every time, without requiring you to babysit it or troubleshoot it or work around its limitations. In the world of peripheral hardware, that kind of consistency is a huge bonus in my line of work. Two for two on Rosonway products. I will be back if I need more ports. I am satisfied with my purchase.

headline: Quality & design issues surfaced during usage
review_text_raw: August 2023 update: On the 3rd week, my 2nd unit started to blink two hard drive connections on and off with only 3 ports switched on. Therefore rating is reduced to 1 star from 2. Initially, my 2nd unit successfully wrote 350 Gb drive to drive across this hub without any buffering errors (buffering errors are what usually goes wrong in such tests). Speed was about 40 - 70 mb per second for nominally-sized files. However was unable to complete a chkdsk on a mounted drive without terminating in a unidentifiable error (again usually what happens with bad hubs). My first unit which was returned had a bad port #3 (counting from the end plugs) and was causing disk errors evident in the Windows event viewer, which actually were errors when chkdsk was used (you cannot always trust the event viewer drive errors as Windows presumes any drive is where you left it from your last Windows session, so if you move it, or it is new to the location on its USD bus, the event viewer will scream bloody murder until it learns the new location, where it will then proclaim the drive is healthy). There appears to be a design deficiency in the hub: on both units I tested, there was too much noise on the final port #10 to plug in a cam. The cam image was very noisy and unusable. Plugging in the cam at the first port works around this design problem. Apparently, there is inadequate noise containment within the hub body, and this can cause slower transfer rates for hard drives and bad images for cams. Given the wide variety of hubs and potential for hub problems, and quality variance of Asian-pacific manufacturers, I am going to keep this one. Be sure to check each port when you receive yours.

product_title: UGREEN USB C Hub 4 Ports, Multiple USB 3.2 Hub, 4x10Gbps Data Transfer
headline: An effective low-cost expander
review_text_raw: I have a relatively new Mac Mini M4, and I do find its ports somewhat limiting. The Mac has two USB-C in front and three Thunderbolt ports in the back. Because the Mac mini itself is so small and light, it can be difficult to access the ports and plug peripherals in and out. This UGreen USB hub works connected either to the USB ports in the front or to one of the Thunderbolt ports in the back. It doesn’t offer Thunderbolt speed, but it is quite quick and responsive for USB-C. I have had minor reliability problems with the ports on the M4—I have a USB keyboard, trackball, backup drive, and sometimes two external SSD drives plugged in, and the Mac itself sometimes doesn’t see everything at the same time—for instance, my trackball sometime disappears. I’ve had this hub plugged into one of the USB-C ports in front and keep a number of peripherals plugged into it, and they have all worked very effectively at the same time, and the speed has been very responsive on the external data drives. So it has improved my Mac. This is not heavy; it’s light plastic, but it works well. What I would have appreciated is if this had one USB-A port, too. I see a lot of USB-A hubs that have one C and a lot of As, but the new standard is USB-C. Some of my peripherals are USB-A, and I have little adapters that convert USB-A to USB-C and those work great with this, too, so with one of those, you can, of course, plug USB-A items into this. This has been very helpful to me with my M4 Mini and I recommend it.

product_title: ACASIS 16 Ports Powered USB 3.2 Hub (8 USB-A 3.2 +8 USB-C 3.2), 10Gbps
headline: Inconsistent, unreliable, and unfortunately disappointing
review_text_raw: I hate to say it, but this hub (at least the one I received) is garbage. I will give the manufacturer points for build quality, the hub seems to built well and using quality materials. Unfortunately, that's about where the positive news ends and as far as usability goes I cannot recommend this device. I've listed below the problems I experienced within the first 24 hours of usage: 1) The switches outright just do not work for many devices. I tried several devices which seem to somehow just "ignore" the switch being turned off. I put ignore in quotes, because the device should not be built in a way that would allow any attached device to communicate with the host while it's off. For some devices, the switch does work correctly. However, for other devices, I can plug a USB cable into the hub and have it persistently connected to the host no matter how many times I toggle the switch on and off. This is a key indicator that the device was not designed in a secure way. When the toggle switch is off, power and connectivity should be completely disconnected to the port. The fact that I am able to bypass the toggle switch is an indicator that some sort of firmware workaround is being used. Bad news here. 2) Power delivery does not seem to work correctly on the hub. I'm using the power adapter that was delivered with the device which is plugged into a stable power source. Some devices which require power delivery (USB-PD) get stuck in an initializing state when drawing power from the hub. They get enough power to appear powered on, but the device never initializes and the host system can detect something was plugged in but cannot interface with the device. When I switch these devices to a different hub (or directly to the host), the issue is not present and the device works as expected. 3) Even devices that do connect, seem to have issues with performance and/or connectivity. When some devices are attached to the hub, the host operating system seems to hang while the device is connecting. I experience this on about 1/3 of my attempts with any mass storage device, and some devices fairly consistently. When I do get a device to connect to the host, my transfer speeds are considerably lower than if I had used a different hub or connected directly to the host. All in all, I absolutely do not recommend this device. There are several clear indicators of poor and unsafe design when it comes to this hub, and I would not trust that it delivers power cleanly or that there's any consistent integrity on file transfers. Again, all of these issues were experienced within the first 24 hours of usage. I tested over a dozen different devices with this hub, of varying types and manufacturer. If I had this many issues straight away, I can guarantee it's not an isolated incident. Even if my hub was "defective", there's no way it would have been defective in a way that would selectively allow some devices to connect while toggled off. Let this be a warning to you!

product_title: Anker Laptop Docking Station Dual Monitor, 8-in-1 USB C Hub with 4K HDMI
headline: The Travel Dock in My Laptop Bag
review_text_raw: What I like Plug-and-play. One USB-C cable in, several ports out. No drivers, no setup, no configuration. HDMI output for plugging into a hotel-room TV or conference projector without an adapter. SD card reader for moving photos off a camera. The microSD reader is a bonus. Two USB-A ports are enough for a mouse, a USB stick, or a card reader I already own. 85 W pass-through charging means I can keep my laptop charged through the hub when I have a USB-C charger handy. Lives in the laptop bag and is ready when I travel. It is the kind of accessory that pays for itself the first time you really need it. Compact and light. I forget it is in the bag until I need it. What annoys me Not a daily driver on my home desk. My home computers already have the ports I need, so the hub sits in the bag most of the time. Bus-powered. No battery, no separate power input. I am not trying to power a hungry external device through it, so this is fine, but it is not a “real docking station” with its own power supply. One HDMI output. If I wanted to drive two external monitors, I would need a different hub or a dock with display-multiplication support. The transcript says “second HDMI port,” and this hub gives me one, not two. No Ethernet port. Wireless works almost everywhere I travel, but a wired Ethernet jack would be a real bonus on hotel networks that block Wi-Fi or charge for it. I do not actually use it on my Mac mini. It would work, but I have not built the habit of plugging the mini through the hub. That is a me problem, not an Anker problem. Who it is for, and who should skip it If you travel with a laptop and need HDMI, an SD card reader, extra USB-A, and the option to charge the laptop through a single cable, this is the right tool. It is small enough to leave in the bag and useful enough to justify its weight. Skip it if you want a full desktop dock with its own power supply, multiple display outputs, Ethernet, and the ability to drive a multi-monitor workstation. That is a different product class, and a single USB-C hub with bus power will not do that job. Skip it if your laptop already has every port you need. The hub is solving a missing-port problem, and if you do not have one, it will just sit in your bag. Verdict The Anker USB-C 7-in-1 hub is a small, useful travel accessory that lives in my laptop bag and earns its place every time I take a trip. It is not exciting. It is not a daily driver. It is the kind of thing that disappears into your workflow and then you are grateful for it when you need it. Grade: A—if you want a single-cable travel dock for a laptop or Mac mini. Buy the linked listing if your use case matches mine.

review_text_raw: As a tech enthusiast and someone who's always on the go, I'm constantly looking for ways to streamline my setup and maximize productivity. The Anker USB-C Hub has become an indispensable tool in my arsenal, transforming my laptop into a versatile workstation wherever I am. Here's why I'm giving it a five-star salute: Connectivity Powerhouse: This compact hub packs a punch with 7 ports: 4K HDMI, 100W Power Delivery, USB-C, 2 USB-A, microSD, and SD card reader. It's like having a mini docking station that fits in the palm of my hand. Crystal-Clear Display: The 4K HDMI port allows me to connect my laptop to an external monitor for a crisp, high-resolution display. It's perfect for presentations, streaming movies, or just expanding my workspace. Blazing-Fast Data Transfer: The USB-C and USB-A ports offer impressive data transfer speeds, making it quick and easy to move files between my devices. No more waiting around for those large files to transfer! Pass-Through Charging: The 100W Power Delivery pass-through charging ensures that my laptop stays powered up while I'm using the hub. This is a lifesaver when I'm working remotely or traveling. Sleek and Portable: The hub's compact and lightweight design makes it incredibly portable. It easily slips into my laptop bag, so I can take it with me wherever I go. A Few Minor Considerations: While I'm extremely happy with the Anker USB-C Hub, there are a couple of minor drawbacks that I've seen mentioned in other reviews: Limited Ethernet: Some users have expressed a desire for an Ethernet port on the hub. Can Get Warm: A few reviewers have mentioned that the hub can get a bit warm during use, especially when transferring large files or using the HDMI port. I've noticed this as well, but it hasn't caused any performance issues. Overall: Despite these minor points, the Anker USB-C Hub is an excellent addition to any tech enthusiast's arsenal. It's a versatile, reliable, and portable solution that expands the capabilities of your laptop and simplifies your workflow.

headline: Flakey with Macs
review_text_raw: I'm the head IT person for my company and, as such, do a lot of IT related purchasing. We have tried a number of USB Docks over the years: some were good; others not so much. So in searching currently available docks, I ran across this one that Amazon kinda of co-branded. Overall Impression I was intrigued because it had a 10 Gbps network connection. That would allow me to make full use of my fiber connection. It also had a 4K HDMI port, good for my 4K monitors. And two high-speed USB connections. This is just enough of everything we typically need/use. I run on a MacBook Pro M3 rich in memory and disk space. When I tested it, I was running Sonoma 14.7 with Sequoia 15.0 having just come available. I never use first release of major OSes, preferring to wait until the .1 release comes along. This gives others time to find the bugs and the vendor to fix them. I plugged it into my Mac. macOS asked for permission to connect the device which I gave it. macOS was happy with the device. I plugged in my monitor's HDMI cable; it connected right up. I plugged in my network cable; it too came right up. I plugged in my Logitech antenna for the detached KB/mouse; that worked. So far, so good. I plugged in a thumb drive and ... nothing. Hmm: that's odd. Plugged it into my Mac directly; worked like a champ. Plugged it back into the dock ... nothing. Not sure of what to make of that other than 2 USB devices and only 1 of the 2 worked. Then I noticed that my 27" 4K LG monitor would randomly turn black, just for a second or two, then would come back on. Okay: that's weird. So I used it a bit and the monitor would turn black now and this in the middle of using it as my main/primary display. It was not like I was pushing out rapid changes such as one would do in a game. I was just using it for normal Outlook, Excel, business type activities. I took it out and plugged in another USB Dock (a Qgeem model that I had been using before) and everything worked perfectly. The monitor went back to being solidly on. My thumb drive showed up just like it should. My external KB/mouse worked like they always have. Pros: - 10G network connection - Decent assortment of ports - Reasonable price - Worked upon plugging in on my Mac (e.g. no drivers to load) Cons: - Flakey USB connections - Flakey monitor connection Recommendation: I would avoid this particular dock, at least for now. Any USB Dock you get needs to be solid and dependable. This one is not. Amazon's vendor that makes it may come up with an improved model sometime in the future. That's then; this is now. There are plenty of USB Docks available. I would search for another brand.

product_title: Razer Huntsman V3 Pro 8KHz Esports Gaming Keyboard, Analog Optical, Black
headline: Adjustable actuation + 8KHz polling: precise control and extremely responsive
review_text_raw: The Razer Huntsman V3 Pro TKL 8KHz is an easy 5-star keyboard for me because of the performance and the level of control it gives you. The biggest highlight is the adjustable actuation: being able to set the exact actuation point (in millimeters) completely changes how the keyboard feels. You can configure it super sensitive so inputs register with a very light press (great for FPS and fast movement), or set a deeper actuation if you want more control and fewer accidental key presses. Key feel is excellent and very consistent. Everything feels fast, stable, and uniform, with a really direct response. For gaming, it shines because you can tune it to your playstyle: with a shorter actuation, strafing, quick direction changes, jumping, and repeated inputs feel more immediate and effortless. And if you tend to mis-press keys, increasing the actuation a bit helps a lot without making the keyboard feel “slow.” On the performance side, the 8KHz polling rate adds to that “instant” feel. It’s not magic, but compared to standard keyboards it does feel more direct and consistent, especially in competitive games where you want inputs to be as fast and repeatable as possible. Customization is another major win. You can create profiles per game and fine-tune different keys differently—for example, setting WASD to a shorter actuation while keeping other keys at a more normal setting. That kind of flexibility makes the keyboard feel tailored instead of one-size-fits-all. Even as a TKL, it’s the ideal format for me: more desk space for mouse movement, better posture, and you still keep everything you actually need for gaming. Build quality is also very good—the keyboard feels solid, well-made, and premium overall. Finally, the design/style I chose (the Niko Edition) looks absolutely beautiful in person and makes the whole setup look even better.

product_title: Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard
headline: Incredible for coding, even better for gaming,
review_text_raw: This one gets reviewed from two angles. As a professional software engineer I live by the quality of my keyboard and have been opinionated about keyboards for more than 20 years, so I ran this as my daily driver for a week to test it out. It was quiet, consistent, and responsive. Despite the gaming branding, this is probably the best tenkeyless keyboard I've ever typed on. Turn the lighting off and it can be dropped onto any office desk without getting a second glance. The high quality PBT keycaps have a texture that doesn't go slick and greasy, and they shouldn't shine up the way ABS does after a few months of heavy use. The switches are factory lubed with a dense foam layer underneath, so there's no hollow plastic rattle and no metallic ping. It's also not the clicking like you get from mechanical switches. It's a low, dull sound that doesn't get annoying in a quiet room or on a call. The adjustable actuation mattered more than I expected for office use. Setting it deeper than a gamer would means you stop firing off accidental characters when your fingers graze the home row, which is something that makes most fast-actuation boards frustrating for long-form writing and code. The aluminum top gives it a solid build, so it doesn't flex or walk across the desk, and the detachable USB-C cable means a longer lifespan. After my week ended I handed it to my teenage son, the gamer, and I really don't think I'm getting it back. He found things I never would have. Rapid Trigger resets the key the instant it starts to rise instead of waiting for a fixed point, which he says completely changes counter-strafing. Snap Tap prioritizes whichever direction key you pressed most recently, so pressing A while holding D doesn't leave you standing there. Dynamic Keystroke lets a single key fire up to four different actions depending on how far down you press it, and Snap Flex assigns one action on press and a different one on release. He set up a key that peeks a corner on a light press and pulls back on release. I didn't even know keyboards did that, but he's raving about it. The 8000Hz polling means it reports to the PC eight times more often than a standard board. He swears he can feel it. I'm skeptical it's perceptible, but he's the one winning matches. All of the tuning lives in the browser based software, which allows you to adjust lighting, actuation and keybinds without installing anything. I really only had two very minor complaints about this keyboard. The switches aren't hot-swappable. Every switch fails eventually, even fancy magnetic switches rated at millions of actuations, and at this price it's disappointing that there's no path to replacing one when it does. The other is the calibration routine that needs to be run every time it's installed or keycaps are replaced, because that part of the software is just tedious and could be better designed. Those are very minor gripes against everything else here. This is a fantastic keyboard, and I'd recommend it without hesitation. Whether you're a professional keyboarder and are looking for a great tenkeyless for daily use, or a gamer looking for an edge, you really can't go wrong with this thing.

Another thing I really love, is this keyboard does have gamepad control mode, meaning it can emulate a gamepad which works really well when I don't want to use my controller, not many HE keyboards have this feature but this keyboard does which was great to see! Overall, I really like this keyboard, I love the 65% layout and the clean design it has, and the build quality is solid, and the features it has is great like the gamepad mode, sure it needs Synapse to customize the settings but I really never had issues with the software even on my other keyboards and mouses and I do like it, call me lucky I don't know, I also like that it came with a really nice 6 foot braided cord which is long enough to reach from my PC way behind my monitor with more to spare. So if you love the design and the 65% layout and hall effect switches, the value you get from this keyboard is great in my opinion, so it does get a solid 5 stars from me, I haven't had an issue yet and I had it for a couple weeks now👍

product_title: Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard
headline: Razer’s Hall Effect Switches Are a Major Improvement
review_text_raw: Razer has made adjustable-actuation keyboards before, but its previous analog Huntsman models relied on optical switches. This is its first real move into the Hall effect keyboard space, and the switch change is not just a spec-sheet distinction. These new magnetic switches feel noticeably smoother and less scratchy than the optical analog switches I have used in the past, especially when pressing a key slowly or typing for longer periods. They also retain a full 4.0mm range of travel, which is less common than I expected among Hall effect gaming keyboards. I can set a very shallow actuation point for movement keys in competitive games without making the entire board feel like a hair trigger. For typing, I prefer a deeper actuation and the full key travel because it feels more natural and gives me fewer accidental inputs. That flexibility makes the Huntsman V3 HE easier to live with as an everyday keyboard rather than something designed exclusively for ranked matches. Rapid trigger works as expected, resetting each key based on movement rather than waiting for it to return to a fixed reset point. In shooters, directional inputs feel crisp and immediate, particularly when rapidly stopping, strafing, or changing direction. Snap Tap can prioritize the newest input between two movement keys, while Snap Flex adds another way to activate commands based on releasing a key. These features will matter most to serious FPS players, but the adjustable actuation is useful even outside competitive gaming. The 8000Hz polling rate gives the keyboard plenty of performance headroom. headline: Hall Effect Makes The Difference
review_text_raw: Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard | Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, 8000 Hz Polling, Razer Snap Flex,Razer Snap Tap, Rapid Trigger, Adjustable Actuation So this listing is for the v3 ten key less Hunstman v3 8K HE keyboard specifically designed for gaming with hall effect switches and snap tap actions. The keyboard has an 8000 Hz polling rate and has onboard memory to store profiles. I have both the v1 and v2 version of this exact keyboard so comparing all three of these keyboards, they all have the exact same solid build quality and sound quality which is a quite thocky experience. The keyboards are solidly built and made of premium material which leads to a very comfortable typing experience. The keyboard is constructed of a solid plastic and metal material which makes them feel premium. The keyboard is about 14" x 5" x 2" high and weighs in with a heft and weight that allows it to sit solidly on your desk. I have been using this keyboard exclusively for nearly two weeks now and it is now my daily driver. I am thoroughly impressed by the HE switches and how very comfortable it is to type on. The software is the one short area as the Synapse software really does not effectively work on Mac but it does sort of work on Windows but don't expect much. The keyboard itself is highly customizable and allows for full customization in color along with key press. Also there is no Linux support either but you can use SignalRGB to control lighting. Also Synapse itself really bogs down your PC and slowly causes a memory leak which means you need to regularly reboot your PC. That being said, the level of customization is something to behold. You can customize everything from tap throw distances to macro's and feature sets. The keyboard can literally be customized by key for color if you want to go through and do that - all though I just keep them one solid color purple for my keyboard. The elevators on the back of the keyboard also help make the keyboard much more comfortable to type on at an angle. The keyboard's compact size really makes it ideal for someone who is limited in space. The price for this keyboard is a premium and is not always the best value for the money but that is not why you are buying this keyboard. This keyboard is designed for someone already in the ecosystem for this keyboard and for the enthusiast who wants the latest and greatest product from the company. Overall I'm very happy with my purchase

product_title: Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard
headline: Elite Magnetic TKL Keyboard With Precision Control
review_text_raw: The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless is engineered as a competitive‐grade keyboard built around Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, offering adjustable actuation from 0.1 mm to 4.0 mm and a 100‐million keystroke lifespan (). This switch architecture eliminates debounce delay entirely, enabling instantaneous actuation and reset behavior that mechanical switches simply cannot match. The magnetic sensing provides exceptionally consistent input recognition, and the keyboard’s internal calibration system compensates for magnetic interference to maintain stable performance over time. Combined with the TKL layout, which frees up desk space for low‐sensitivity mouse movement, the Huntsman V3 HE is clearly designed for players who rely on precision micro‐adjustments and rapid directional changes. One of the most defining features is Rapid Trigger, which allows keys to reset the moment they begin to rise rather than waiting for a fixed reset point. This dramatically increases responsiveness in FPS titles, enabling faster counter‐strafes, smoother movement corrections, and more reliable repeated inputs. Esports.gg’s testing highlights how Rapid Trigger transforms WASD control, making movement feel “snappy, predictable, and extremely responsive” — a sentiment that aligns with real‐world gameplay impressions. The keyboard also supports Dynamic Keystroke, allowing up to four actions on a single key at different actuation depths, and Snap Flex, which assigns one action on press and another on release. These features give competitive players granular control over movement, utility activation, and complex keybind setups, especially in games like Valorant, CS2, and Apex Legends (). The Huntsman V3 HE’s 8000 Hz HyperPolling is another major technical advantage. With true 8000 Hz performance, the keyboard sends input data to the PC eight times more frequently than standard 1000 Hz keyboards, reducing average latency to 0.60 ms — roughly 8% faster than competing high‐end boards (). In fast‐paced shooters, this reduction in input delay contributes to more immediate movement and firing responses. Esports.gg’s analysis notes that the keyboard feels “instantaneous,” with no perceptible delay between keypress and on‐screen action. For competitive players who rely on tight timing windows, this level of responsiveness provides a measurable advantage. Build quality is another strong point. The keyboard uses a 5052 aluminum alloy top case, which gives it a rigid, premium feel while keeping weight manageable for LAN events. The switches are factory‐lubricated, and a dense internal foam layer improves acoustics, reducing hollow resonance and delivering a smoother, more muted sound profile. The doubleshot PBT keycaps resist shine and wear, maintaining texture even under heavy daily use. The detachable USB‐C cable and hybrid onboard storage for up to six profiles add practical flexibility, especially for players who switch between systems or travel frequently (). Razer’s software approach is also noteworthy. The Huntsman V3 HE supports Synapse for Web, allowing users to adjust actuation, Rapid Trigger sensitivity, polling rate, lighting, and keybinds directly through a browser without installing software — ideal for tournament environments or shared PCs. The keyboard’s Chroma RGB is bright and evenly diffused, and while lighting is not the focus of this model, it integrates cleanly with competitive setups. Real‐world impressions consistently highlight the keyboard’s stability, predictable actuation behavior, and the immediate improvement in movement control during gameplay. Overall, the Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless delivers exceptional responsiveness, deep customization, durable construction, and esports‐grade precision. Its combination of Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, Rapid Trigger, Dynamic Keystroke, Snap Tap, and true 8000 Hz HyperPolling makes it one of the most technically advanced competitive keyboards available. For players who prioritize movement accuracy, instant input recognition, and customizable actuation, this keyboard offers a genuine performance advantage that is immediately noticeable in high‐speed FPS environments.

product_title: Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard
headline: Maybe im ready to give Razer another chance
review_text_raw: The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini keyboard is the latest addition to their Hall Effect Magnetic keyboard lineup. If you haven't been keeping up with keyboard technologies, compared to traditional keyboard switches made by companies like Cherry, they are now utilizing magnets and lasers to create a much more responsive key press reducing latency and allowing for customizable key actuation based on the users preference. I am a hobbyist with keyboard tech, where I have built a good variety of keyboards with DIY kits, customized some of my own, and tend to go out of my way to try new technologies. This is my third time trying a Hall Effect keyboard, with my first being the Steelseries Apex Pro ( with HyperMagnetic switches) and the original Razer Huntsman. I didn't hold onto either of those keyboards very long as at the time they were very expensive compared to their traditional counterparts. They also didn't wow me out of the box with their switch technology. Keypresses felt weak, as if there was no feedback to register that I had hit a key. It also took a lot of tweaking to get them to what I would consider a usable state with accurate typing. Which leaves me with the new Razer Huntsman, where I am happy to report it doesn't share any of these problems. The recent revisions have made many changes, improving the texture on the keycaps, the sound of the keypresses, the out of box actuation is exactly what I want, and the 8khz polling is probably helping with how responsive the keys feel. I generally use full size keyboards as I like to have a numpad, but the feel of this keyboard is winning me over to make it my daily driver away from my Mountain Everest Max with Cherry Blues. Lubed Holy Panda switches are the only ones I own that might feel a little bit better than these, but the overall responsiveness of these HE Magentics is something I haven't had the pleasure of experiencing before. My closing statement will be that I started my PC peripheral journey with Razer back when they released the first Blackwidow keyboard & OG Razer Naga. I have watched their products go through sharp declines, and had a time of regret after recommending them to several friends and watching their mice break down on them within a year each. I am hesitant to recommend them again due to the many issues I have had across a few years before ultimately moving away from their products entirely. I will update this review if I encounter any issues with the keyboard as I daily drive it. Post note: I forgot to mention Synapse in this review, as I don't really want to use it. I will add it in if I change my mind but luckily the keyboard works fine without it. Windows Dynamic Lighting isn't working with the keyboard out of the box but I know of other 3rd party software that used to work with Razer that I preferred. After one pop up the Razer software installer hasn't appeared again which is nice.

product_title: Logitech G413 SE Full-Size Mechanical Gaming Keyboard - Black
headline: Worth 60 bucks easy, on sale it's an absolute bargain.
review_text_raw: I ordered one of these after my place of employment got tired of keyboards failing constantly. After several months of outright abusive use by my co-workers, they still performed flawlessly with a lovely sense of tactile feedback, soda spills aside. One failed only after half a thermos of coffee was spilled into it, but that's to be expected from anything not waterproof rated. After ordering one for myself to use at home, I LOVE typing on it. It's my first true mechanical keyboard, and it's pleasant to just tap away, typing whatever I feel like. Each key feels like it's got two levels of depression (almost like me): First a clear 'catch' when the key activates and types, and then another more firm one when you reach the bottom of the key well. I've yet to have it double-type anything even when my clumsy fingers wanted to, although it hasn't saved me from butterfingering my keystrokes in games. As far as gaming goes, it's not PERFECT. It does make an audible noise when typing, so when you are frantically spamming the strafe or jump keys, it's going to sound like clicking the mouse over and over, but it's really no worse than your average mouse. If you're wearing headphones and blasting your speakers, you won't notice it. If you're in a silent small room, you can't avoid hearing it. Find your medium. Its clearly more meant for office work, but I find it good for gaming, and it's sturdy and heavy enough it doesn't move around at all or feel like it'll die if I drop my phone on it.

headline: Not the best choice for Mac; satisfying click but not for quiet environments
review_text_raw: I can't tell you how well this works for gaming, but if you're looking to buy this as a Mac keyboard for standard daily use, definitely read on. This keyboard is far better for a PC. It doesn't have matching keys for a Mac keyboard, so you'll have reduced functionality with key commands. These are differences I've come across so far: - Instead of a CMD key on both sides of the space bar, this keyboard has only one on the left of the spacebar that functions that way, and it's not in the position of the usual Mac CMD key. (see my pic) - There's no volume control on this keyboard, so you'll have to have your Mac keyboard available to change volume unless you keep volume control visible on your menu bar. - Screen dimming requires holding this keyboard's fn key and then using F1 or F2. - Some special function keys on this keyboard don't do anything on a Mac. Here's what I do like about the keyboard: - Satisfying click. The keys are like old school keyboards with large keys that actually had feel to them. The volume of the click is kind of loud though, so if you need to maintain a quieter environment this keyboard won't do. - The attached 10 key is nice to have. - It's corded so no batteries required. - The keyboard is sturdy feeling with just-right weight to it - The key backlighting is adjustable - No quick trigger keys means no accidental double lettering - Because the keyboard rises high off your desktop compared to modern keyboards, make sure you have a seating position that lets you keep your hands lower than normal. Overall this keyboard is probably great for gaming or for PC users who don't have to keep it down while using it. If you're a Mac user, especially one who needs a quiet environment, you should look at different models.

headline: Love it!

product_title: AULA F99 Wireless Mechanical Keyboard,Tri-Mode BT5.0/2.4GHz/USB-C Hot Swappable Custom Keyboard,Pre-lubed Linear Switches,RGB Backlit Computer Gaming Keyboards for PC/Tablet/PS/Xbox
headline: Great keyboard for the price
review_text_raw: The Aula F99 is a "96%" mechanical keyboard that comes in around the $90 price point normally, but can get as low as $60 on sale. That form factor means that it does have a numpad and arrow keys as well as home, delete and page up/down keys, but those keys are moved up in-line with the function keys and the numpad/arrow keys are squished up closer to the main keys with the arrow keys set a little further down to make space. Having a numpad was a must for me because I like to play games that often use the numpad for important functions, and I also prefer typing numbers on a numpad when the occasion arises. At this price point, this is probably one of the best options for people who want a numpad and/or arrow keys but still want a keyboard that looks and sounds more like a custom keyboard you see in YouTube shorts of people doing sound tests. It has linear switches meaning there's no "bump" or clickiness to them, I'm not 100% sure what exact switches they are because there is some conflicting information online. I think mine has "Star Vector" switches? Regardless, the switches are quite light on force and very quiet, which brings us to the sound. This keyboard sounds great for the price. It's a little on the clacky side, but the switches have no scratchiness to them and are obviously pre-lubed, and there appears to be some kind of sound-deadening material inside the case as there is none of that hollow pinginess you get from something like a cheap Logitech mechanical. Overall it is a massive improvement from the Logitech keyboard I had previously to this one. The case is plastic but seems to be fairly high quality. The keyboard is surprisingly heavy which is very confidence inspiring and gives you a very stable feeling typing experience. It also has RGB lighting on all of the keys but the keycaps are not shine-through meaning the lettering doesn't light up. If that's a big deal to you, I'm sure you could swap them out for something else later as it does come with a keycap and switch puller, which also means you can change the switches if you want. It also has 3 different connection modes: "Wired" which uses a USB-C port on the board for connection (and it does come with a USB-C to A cable in the box), "2.4 GHz" which uses a little wireless dongle that sits in a little slot on the top edge of the board when not in use, and it's also able to connect via bluetooth. I haven't tested the battery life as I use this keyboard at my desktop computer with the wired connection, but having the different modes and a physical switch to change between them means you could have this board connected to multiple different devices and switch between them whenver you want which is cool and useful if you need that. I'm fairly new to the world of mechanical keyboards, this is only the second one I've ever owned, the first being a Logitech board that didn't sound or feel nearly as good as this one. As I type this review out on this very keyboard, I find myself liking the sound and feeling more and more. I'm sure there are things about it that someone with more knowledge and experience could pick apart and criticize, but overall I am very happy with this keyboard and would definitely recommend it to anyone who's not an expert and is looking for something better than the offerings from companies like Logitech and Razer.

product_title: Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini 65% 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard
headline: Incredible for coding, even better for gaming,
review_text_raw: This one gets reviewed from two angles. As a professional software engineer I live by the quality of my keyboard and have been opinionated about keyboards for more than 20 years, so I ran this as my daily driver for a week to test it out. It was quiet, consistent, and responsive. Despite the gaming branding, this is probably the best tenkeyless keyboard I've ever typed on. Turn the lighting off and it can be dropped onto any office desk without getting a second glance. The high quality PBT keycaps have a texture that doesn't go slick and greasy, and they shouldn't shine up the way ABS does after a few months of heavy use. The switches are factory lubed with a dense foam layer underneath, so there's no hollow plastic rattle and no metallic ping. It's also not the clicking like you get from mechanical switches. It's a low, dull sound that doesn't get annoying in a quiet room or on a call. The adjustable actuation mattered more than I expected for office use. Setting it deeper than a gamer would means you stop firing off accidental characters when your fingers graze the home row, which is something that makes most fast-actuation boards frustrating for long-form writing and code. The aluminum top gives it a solid build, so it doesn't flex or walk across the desk, and the detachable USB-C cable means a longer lifespan. After my week ended I handed it to my teenage son, the gamer, and I really don't think I'm getting it back. He found things I never would have. Rapid Trigger resets the key the instant it starts to rise instead of waiting for a fixed point, which he says completely changes counter-strafing. Snap Tap prioritizes whichever direction key you pressed most recently, so pressing A while holding D doesn't leave you standing there. Dynamic Keystroke lets a single key fire up to four different actions depending on how far down you press it, and Snap Flex assigns one action on press and a different one on release. He set up a key that peeks a corner on a light press and pulls back on release. I didn't even know keyboards did that, but he's raving about it. The 8000Hz polling means it reports to the PC eight times more often than a standard board. He swears he can feel it. I'm skeptical it's perceptible, but he's the one winning matches. All of the tuning lives in the browser based software, which allows you to adjust lighting, actuation and keybinds without installing anything. I really only had two very minor complaints about this keyboard. The switches aren't hot-swappable. Every switch fails eventually, even fancy magnetic switches rated at millions of actuations, and at this price it's disappointing that there's no path to replacing one when it does. The other is the calibration routine that needs to be run every time it's installed or keycaps are replaced, because that part of the software is just tedious and could be better designed. Those are very minor gripes against everything else here. This is a fantastic keyboard, and I'd recommend it without hesitation. Whether you're a professional keyboarder and are looking for a great tenkeyless for daily use, or a gamer looking for an edge, you really can't go wrong with this thing.
